text: Owner, group, everyone else — that's the entire rwx model, and it runs out of road the moment you need a second user or a second group with different access to the same file. This lesson covers the real fix: Access Control Lists, read and set with getfacl and setfacl, plus the sticky bit that protects a shared, world-writable directory like /tmp from users deleting each other's files.

getfacl prints every permission entry on a file, starting with the same owner, group, and other you already know. setfacl -m u:auditor:r-- report.csv adds a named user entry beyond those three — auditor gets read access without joining the file's group at all — and setfacl -m g:qa:rw- does the same for a second group. Either command rewrites the ACL; getfacl always shows you the current full list.

A file with an ACL shows a trailing + after its permission string in ls -l — the signal there's more to see with getfacl. The mask entry caps the ceiling: even if a named user or group entry grants more, nothing beyond mask actually applies, and setfacl recalculates it automatically unless you tell it not to. setfacl -x removes one named entry; setfacl -b strips every ACL entry back to plain rwx.

/tmp is deliberately world-writable so any user or process can drop a temp file there — but plain write permission on a directory also means you can delete or rename anything inside it, which would let any user wipe out anyone else's files. The sticky bit closes that: inside a sticky directory, only a file's owner, or root, can delete or rename it, no matter who else can write to the directory itself.

That trailing t in drwxrwxrwt is the sticky bit, set with chmod +t or an octal mode starting with a leading 1, like chmod 1777. Next up: scheduling work safely — real crontab syntax, systemd timers as the modern alternative, and the privilege-escalation risk a world-writable scheduled script actually creates.
